title: Abuse & Anti-Fraud in Design
summary: Designing the system to resist bots and abuse from day one — quotas, audit trails, and minimizing the personal data you even collect — rather than bolting on defenses after an incident.

slides.markdown:
Abuse resistance is easy to treat as a feature you add later — a captcha here, a rate limit there — after the first incident forces the issue. Designed in from day one, it's cheaper and far more effective: quotas, audit trails, and bot-signal checks as first-class parts of the architecture, not patches bolted onto a request pipeline that never expected them.

This topic covers abuse defense as a design concern: where signal checks sit in the request path, how quotas and audit trails get built in rather than retrofitted, and why collecting less personal data in the first place is itself a defense.

slides.sectionTitle: Bot and abuse defense as an architectural concern
slides.markdown:
Rate limits, challenge flows (captchas, step-up verification), and device signals are usually thought of as security features, but where they sit in the architecture is a design decision with real cost trade-offs. Checking too late — after a request has already hit the database — wastes resources on requests you were always going to reject. Checking too early, with too little context, blocks legitimate users who look unusual for reasons that have nothing to do with abuse.

The common pattern is a **layered pipeline**: cheap, coarse signals (IP reputation, request rate) filter first at the edge, and only requests that pass move on to more expensive, more accurate checks (device fingerprinting, behavioral signals) closer to the action being protected. Design this pipeline explicitly rather than sprinkling checks wherever they seemed convenient to add.

slides.sectionTitle: Per-tenant and per-user quotas as a design primitive
slides.markdown:
A quota — a hard cap on how much of something a user or tenant can do in a window — is easiest to add when it's part of the original data model, and painful to retrofit once every service assumes unlimited usage. Building it in from the start means every write path that matters (account creation, message sends, API calls) checks and increments a counter as part of the same transaction, not as an afterthought bolted on with a separate service that can drift out of sync.

Quotas also need a **default deny posture at the edges**: a new account or an unusual pattern gets a conservative quota by default, with the ability to raise it explicitly for trusted, verified users — rather than starting everyone unlimited and trying to catch abuse after the fact.

This is one of the cheapest anti-abuse investments available, and one of the most expensive to add after a system already assumes unlimited usage everywhere.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: an abuse-signal check inserted before the core request path
slides.markdown:
A request enters the system and hits an **abuse-signal check** — IP reputation, rate limit, device signal — *before* it reaches the core business logic (checkout, login, message send). Requests that fail this check are rejected or challenged immediately, without ever touching the database or downstream services that the abuse was actually targeting.

Only requests that pass proceed to the core path. This ordering matters: it protects the expensive parts of the system from ever seeing the bulk of abusive traffic, rather than absorbing the load and rejecting it deep inside the stack.

slides.sectionTitle: Audit trails: designing for "who did what, when" before you need it
slides.markdown:
An audit trail that gets added after an incident is usually missing exactly the field you need to answer the question that matters. Designing it up front means every sensitive action — a delete, a permission change, a data export — writes an immutable record: who, what, on which resource, when, and from where, stored separately from the data it describes so the record survives even if the underlying row is deleted.

The test for a good audit design is a concrete question, not a vague goal: can you answer "who deleted this specific row, and when" in seconds, not by grepping through application logs that were never meant for this purpose. If the answer requires reconstructing intent from scattered logs, the audit trail wasn't designed, it accumulated.

slides.sectionTitle: PII minimization: designing to collect and retain the least data that does the job
slides.markdown:
The cheapest way to reduce the damage of a future breach is to not have the data in the first place. **PII minimization** means designing each feature to ask: does this genuinely need a user's phone number, exact birthdate, or precise location, or would a coarser or absent value do the same job?

This extends to retention: data collected for a legitimate reason (fraud checks at signup, say) doesn't need to be kept forever once that reason has passed — a deliberate deletion or anonymization schedule is part of the design, not a compliance afterthought.

Minimization is also an anti-fraud measure in its own right: data you never collected can't leak, can't be subpoenaed, and can't be the target of the exact kind of scraping or credential-stuffing abuse this topic is about.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: blocking in real time vs flagging for async review
slides.markdown:
Not every suspicious signal deserves the same response speed.

| | Block in real time | Flag for async review |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | Immediate — request rejected or challenged before it completes | Request proceeds; a human or later job reviews afterward |
| False-positive cost | High — a wrong call blocks a legitimate user immediately | Low — legitimate users aren't affected in the moment |
| Best fit | High-confidence signals (known bad IP, failed device check) | Ambiguous signals that need context — unusual but not clearly malicious |
| Risk if used wrong | Blocking on weak signals frustrates real users | Reviewing too late lets damage accumulate before action |

**How to decide:** reserve real-time blocking for high-confidence signals where a false positive is cheap to recover from; route ambiguous signals to async review so a human or a slower model can add context a millisecond decision can't afford.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: an audit log that exists but can't answer the question fast enough to matter
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We log everything, so we have an audit trail."

**Why it's wrong:** application logs built for debugging are usually scattered across services, rotate out after days or weeks, and mix operational noise with the one action that actually matters. When an incident happens and someone asks "who deleted this row, and when," the honest answer is often "we'd have to grep through log aggregation across six services and hope the retention window didn't already expire."

**Correct model:** treat audit logging as a distinct, deliberately-designed system — a dedicated, append-only record of sensitive actions with a long retention window, indexed by resource and actor, separate from operational debug logs. The test is concrete: can you answer "who did this, when" in seconds, not after an afternoon of log archaeology.
